evals.prompt: After a successful login our callback page restores the user's destination with `const next = params.get('returnTo'); if (next?.startsWith('/')) router.replace(next);`. A tester reports that `/login?returnTo=//attacker.example/pay` sends them off-site after they authenticate, and support says users are landing on a lookalike page still holding a fresh session. Give the smallest fix.
evals.expected_output: Identifies the auth-specific `returnTo` contract failure: `startsWith('/')` accepts protocol-relative `//host` and other parser tricks, so the post-authentication navigation becomes an open redirect at the highest-trust moment of the flow. Fixes by resolving and validating the destination or mapping it to an allowlisted route, and routes the generic open-redirect URL-parsing primitive to frontend-security-baseline.
expectations: The response explains that `//attacker.example/pay` passes a `startsWith('/')` check because a protocol-relative URL begins with a slash, so the string check is not a same-origin check.
It frames the harm in auth terms: the redirect fires after the session is established, so the user arrives at an attacker-controlled page in an authenticated state.

The smallest fix resolves the value against the current origin (for example `new URL(next, location.origin)`) and requires a same-origin result, or replaces the free-form URL with a server-known key mapped to an allowlisted internal route.
It preserves the actual product contract — the intended destination is still restored on success — rather than dropping `returnTo` support entirely.
The generic open-redirect and URL-allowlist security primitive, including any server-side validation of the destination, is routed to frontend-security-baseline.
It names the flow test to add: a cold direct navigation to `/login?returnTo=//attacker.example/pay` must authenticate and land on a safe in-app destination.

evals.prompt: Security review flagged that our SPA keeps the access JWT in `localStorage`, set by the login component right after `POST /login` returns. Please treat this as an auth-flow contract defect and rewrite the login form component to fix it.
evals.expected_output: Declines to own the finding: token storage, cookie attributes, SameSite, and CSRF primitives belong to frontend-security-baseline, and rewriting the login form does not change where the token lives. States what would make it an auth-flow finding instead.
expectations: The response states that token/session storage and cookie attributes are owned by frontend-security-baseline, not by this skill, and routes the finding there.
It points out that the defect is the storage decision and the server session design, so editing the login form component is the wrong lever.

It names what would turn this into a real auth-flow contract finding: client-only logout that leaves the server session valid, sign-in state that survives an expired session with no recovery, a login error that enumerates which accounts exist, or a missing fresh-verification step before a sensitive account change.
It does not invent a backend cryptography or session-token-format recommendation, since that is explicitly outside this skill.
It offers the auth-flow work it can legitimately do on this login page — autocomplete fields, generic error copy, retry and expiry states — as a separate, smaller deliverable.

evals.prompt: Email verification links like `https://app.example/verify?token=…&returnTo=/projects/42/settings` open the app but always land on the dashboard instead of the deep destination. Our fix was to read `returnTo` inside the `/verify` route component and call `router.replace()` after the token exchange resolves. It still lands on the dashboard on a cold open from the mail client, though it works when we navigate there from inside the app. What are we missing?
evals.expected_output: Recognizes the obvious in-flow fix is blocked upstream: on a cold direct navigation the router is not yet ready and the app performs its own default redirect before the verify component reads the query, so the auth-specific restore never gets a chance to run. Routes router readiness and cold-URL reconstruction to deeplink-hydration while keeping the `returnTo` validation contract here.
expectations: The response identifies that the failure only reproduces on cold direct navigation, which points at router or app readiness rather than at the token-exchange logic.
It explains that a default post-boot redirect or an unready router can consume the navigation before the verify component parses `returnTo`, so calling `router.replace()` later cannot win the race.
Router readiness, cold direct-navigation entry, and URL-to-screen reconstruction are routed to deeplink-hydration as the blocking condition this skill cannot fix from inside the verify component.
This skill retains the auth-specific part: validating the restored destination before navigating, and defining the expired, already-used, and invalid-token states for the verification link.
It asks for the concrete cold-open evidence — what the URL is at first paint and whether the redirect happens before or after the token exchange — instead of guessing at a fix.
The recommended test enters from a cold URL rather than navigating in-app, since the in-app path already passes.

evals.prompt: Android users say the SMS code never autofills in our one-time-code screen. iPhone users have no complaints. A teammate says the fix is one line: add `autocomplete="one-time-code"` to the input. Ship it?
evals.expected_output: Corrects the mechanism rather than accepting the one-line claim: `autocomplete="one-time-code"` is the right hint and is what iOS/macOS Safari autofills from, but Android Chrome's SMS retrieval needs the WebOTP API plus a correctly formatted message, so the attribute alone will not fix the reported platform.
expectations: The response keeps `autocomplete="one-time-code"` as correct and worth having, and notes it is the hint iOS and macOS Safari autofill from — which is consistent with iPhone users not complaining.

It states that Android Chrome's SMS code retrieval comes from the WebOTP API (`navigator.credentials.get({ otp: { transport: ['sms'] } })`), which is additive to the attribute rather than implied by it.
It notes the WebOTP path also depends on the SMS body carrying the origin-bound suffix, so the message format is part of the contract and not purely a frontend change.
It asks for the concrete platform evidence before shipping — which Android browser and version, whether the attribute is already present, and what the delivered SMS body looks like.
It keeps the surrounding flow contract in view: expiry, resend, and retry state for the code, and a fallback path when autofill does not fire at all.
Native form-validity wiring for the invalid-code message — the Constraint Validation API, `setCustomValidity()`, and `:user-invalid` timing — is routed to constraint-validation-contracts.
